name: Asa (son of Abijah)
title: The Reforming King of Judah
summary: Asa reigned over Judah for 41 years and was one of the kingdom's most prominent kings in the struggle against idolatry. With resolute action he cleared the land of foreign cult objects, and he showed unusual principle when he removed his own grandmother Maaka from her position as queen mother because of her idol. His trust in God was tested when a powerful Cushite army under Zerah marched against Judah – Asa threw himself to the Lord in prayer and experienced an overwhelming victory. The prophet Azariah then encouraged him to hold fast to the reform course. Nevertheless, his legacy is overshadowed by the final years of his reign: when Baasha of Israel threatened, Asa chose political pragmatism and allied himself with Ben-Hadad king of Aram instead of seeking God's guidance, something the prophet Hanani confronted him about. When a serious illness struck him toward the end of his life, he turned exclusively to human help. Asa's life paints a moving picture of both the strength and frailty of faith – a king who began with wholehearted devotion but ended with failing trust.

keyEvents.title: Religious Reforms
keyEvents.description: Asa removed the foreign altars, broke down the sacred pillars, and cut down the Asherah poles. He commanded Judah to seek the Lord and keep his law and commandments, even though the high places were not completely removed.

keyEvents.title: Victory over the Cushite Zerah
keyEvents.description: When the Cushite Zerah advanced against Judah with an overwhelming army, Asa cried out to the Lord and achieved a miraculous victory. He confessed his complete dependence on God.

keyEvents.title: The Prophet Azariah's Encouragement
keyEvents.description: After the victory, the prophet Azariah, son of Oded, met with King Asa and encouraged him to continue his reforms, saying: 'The Lord is with you as long as you are with Him.' Asa accepted this message and intensified his reform efforts.

keyEvents.title: Removal of Queen Mother Maacah
keyEvents.description: Asa removed his own grandmother Maacah from her position as queen mother because she had made an abhorrent Asherah image. He destroyed the image and burned it by the Kidron Brook.

keyEvents.title: Alliance with Ben-Hadad Against Israel
keyEvents.description: When Baasha of Israel built the fortress of Ramah to block Judah, Asa formed an alliance with Ben-Hadad of Aram by sending treasures from the temple, instead of relying on the Lord. The prophet Hanani rebuked him for this.

keyEvents.title: Illness and Death
keyEvents.description: In his 39th year as king, Asa was afflicted with a serious foot disease but sought help only from physicians, not from the Lord. He died after reigning for 41 years and was buried with great honor in the City of David.

versions.summary: Asa was the third king of Judah following the division of the kingdom and reigned for 41 years. He carried out extensive religious reforms, removed idolatry, and sought the Lord. Despite a strong start, he showed weakness toward the end of his reign by relying on human help rather than God.
versions.title: The Reforming King of Judah
versions.reason: [minor] Asa was not merely a general 'leader', but specifically a religious reformer. Adding 'reformer' provides a more precise description of his role.; [major] Maacah (Ma'aka) is referred to in 2 Chronicles 15:16 as Asa's 'mother', but she was actually his grandmother – she was the mother of Abijam/Abijah (1 Kings 15:2). It is possible that she continued to serve as queen mother during Asa's reign. The field should reflect this nuance, either by retaining 'Maacah' with an explanation or by noting that his biological mother is unknown.; [minor] The expression 'Asherah poles' should be considered. The usual Norwegian form is 'Asherah pillars' or 'Asherah poles'. Consistency in terminology is recommended.; [major] Footnotes are completely missing. For a profile of this complexity, historical, archaeological, and theological footnotes should be included – for example, regarding the identity of Zerah, Maacah's role as queen mother, and archaeological findings related to Asa's reign.; [minor] The period c. 913–873 BC likely represents his reign rather than his full lifespan. It should be clarified that this is the regnal period, not birth and death dates.

versions.summary: Asa was the third king of Judah following the division of the kingdom and reigned for 41 years. He carried out extensive religious reforms, removed idolatry, and sought the Lord with wholehearted zeal. He showed great courage in removing his own grandmother Maacah from her position as queen mother due to her idolatry. Despite a strong start, he showed weakness toward the end of his reign by seeking a military alliance with Aram instead of trusting God, and by failing to seek the Lord during his illness.
versions.title: The Reforming King of Judah
versions.reason: [minor] The word 'helhjertad' is the Swedish spelling. The correct Norwegian is 'helhjertet'.; [major] Maaka was not Asa's mother, but his grandmother (paternal). She was the mother of Abijah. Asa's actual mother is not named in the Bible. The field should either be set to zero or explained with a footnote. Alternatively, one could list 'Maaka' but clarify that she was the grandmother; however, for data consistency, it is better to set mother to zero since Maaka was the grandmother, not the mother.; [minor] The text states that Asa removed the high places, but 2 Chron 15:17 and 1 Kings 15:14 indicate that the high places were not completely removed. 2 Chron 14:4-5 can be interpreted as him attempting to remove them, while it is later clarified that they were not entirely removed. The description should be nuanced.; [minor] 'The Ethiopian Zerah' should preferably be written as 'the Cushite Zerah' or 'Zerah from Cush' to more accurately reflect the Hebrew text (Zerakh ha-Kushi). 'Ethiopian' is a modern term that can be misleading.

versions.summary: Asa was the third king of Judah after the division of the kingdom and reigned for 41 years. He implemented extensive religious reforms, fought against idolatry, and sought the Lord with wholehearted zeal. He showed great courage by removing his own grandmother Maaka from her position as queen mother because of her idol. When an overwhelming Cushite army threatened the kingdom, he placed his trust in God and achieved a miraculous victory. However, toward the end of his reign, his trust faltered: he formed a military alliance with Aram instead of relying on the Lord, and when he was struck by serious illness, he sought only human help. Asa's life illustrates the tension between faithful reliance on God and the temptation to depend on human resources.

footnotes.text: Maacah (also spelled Ma'akah) is described as Asa's 'mother' in the biblical text, but she was actually his grandmother—the mother of Abijah/Abijam (1 Kings 15:2). The fact that she retained the title 'queen mother' (Hebrew: gevira) into her grandson's reign demonstrates the significant political power this role held in the Old Testament monarchy.

The identity of 'the Cushite Zerah' (Hebrew: Zerakh ha-Kushi) is debated. Some scholars have attempted to identify him with the Egyptian pharaoh Osorkon I of the 22nd dynasty, while others believe he was a Cushite military commander. The enormous army size described as 'a thousand times a thousand' (one million) uses a typical Semitic expression for an overwhelmingly large force.

Archaeological findings from the kingdom of Judah during this period show signs of religious reform activity that correspond with the biblical accounts of Asa's reforms. Among other things, destroyed cultic objects from this time have been discovered in several excavations throughout Judah.

The Hebrew word for Asa's foot disease is unclear, but rabbinic sources have speculated it may have been gout or a form of peripheral vascular disease. The Talmud (Sotah 10a) discusses Asa's illness in the context of his spiritual condition, and several rabbis view the disease as a consequence of his forcing people into labor (1 Kings 15:22).

Ben-Hadad of Aram-Damascus (Hebrew: Ben-Hadad, 'son of [the god] Hadad') is mentioned in several extra-biblical sources, including the Melqart stele found near Aleppo. The alliance between Asa and Ben-Hadad illustrates the complex diplomatic maneuvering among the small states of the Levant during this period.

The role of the Gevira (Queen Mother) in ancient Judah was a formal and influential position, likely with its own ceremonial and political privileges. The fact that Asa found it necessary to formally remove Maakah from this office underscores both the power of the position and the seriousness of his reforms.

Asa's 41-year reign makes him one of the longest-reigning kings in Judah. The chronology of his reign (c. 911–870 BC) is based on cross-synchronization between the king lists of Judah and Israel, as well as correlation with Assyrian eponym lists that provide fixed chronological anchors.
